activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: When a phone takes a photo with location services on, it can write the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken into hidden data in the file, called EXIF metadata.
story:
Oliver was halfway through his pretzel when Zach leaned across the food court table and said, "Check this out." Zach held up his phone, showing a photo of his brand new gaming setup: three monitors, glowing keyboard, a wall of posters. "Posted it this morning. Twenty likes already."

"Cool," said Oliver, though his eyes had caught something else. At the edge of the shot, half cut off by the doorframe, was a whiteboard with Zach's wifi password written on it in fat blue marker. Oliver had seen it once when he was over at Zach's house, and he had copied it down himself that day so his tablet could get online in the den.

"You okay?" Zach asked. "You look like you bit your pretzel wrong."

"I did," Oliver lied, and swallowed. He remembered the mall's free wifi kiosk near the escalators, the one with the big sign that said it could generate a personal passcode for every visitor. That got him thinking about passwords and how they travel around, and that got him thinking about what else travels around with a photo. He had read something once, a few months back, about hidden data in picture files. At the time it had seemed boring, like reading about car engines. Now it did not seem boring at all.

"Send me the actual photo," Oliver said. "The file, not the post."

"Why?"

"Science project."

Zach rolled his eyes but shared it. Oliver opened the picture in his phone's details view, the way the article had described, and there it was: a little map with a pin on it. The pin sat on the exact corner of Maple and Third, two houses down from Zach's front door. He scrolled further and found the numbers too, long strings of decimals that had to be coordinates. When a phone takes a photo with location services on, it can write the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken into hidden data in the file, called EXIF metadata. Zach had never mentioned that word to him. Oliver read it on the screen twice: EXIF.

"Zach," Oliver said, keeping his voice level, "how many strangers liked that post?"

"Twenty. Why?"

"Twenty strangers can open that photo and see a map pin on your street. Your house is basically on the map. And your wifi password is on your whiteboard in the corner."

Zach grabbed the phone back and stared. His thumb hovered over the screen. "Marco liked it too, but the rest are people I don't know. There's some account called skaterdude44 that likes everything I post."

Oliver remembered Marco, who had once applied to be a candidate for student council treasurer and had made everyone promise not to post his speech video until he'd practiced more. Marco understood this stuff, or at least he worried about it, which might be the same thing. "Text Marco," Oliver said. "He'll know how to strip the location off."

"I could just delete the post," Zach said slowly.

"That works too."

Zach deleted it. Then he sat there turning his phone over in his hands, the way he did when a math problem refused to break open. "Was it dumb to post it?" he asked.

Oliver thought about all the photos he had ever sent, the ones from his own room, his backyard, his grandmother's porch. He had never checked a single one for hidden data. "I don't know," he said. "Maybe just dumb to leave the location on."

The pretzel had gone cold. Zach finally typed a message to Marco, and they both watched the little dots blink while the escalators hummed behind them. Marco's reply popped up: "Turning off location services in settings works too. Want me to come to the mall and show you?"

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Knowing a word's language of origin can help with spelling: the 'k' sound in 'chorus' is spelled 'ch' because it comes from Greek, while the 'sh' in 'chef' comes from French.
story:
The community center gym smelled like floor wax and popcorn, and the folding chairs were already full when Caleb checked in at the sign-up table. Ms. Almeida, who ran the Tuesday study group, handed him a numbered card. "You're fourteen," she said. "Number fourteen. Don't lose it."

Athena and Cheikh were in the third row, saving him a seat until the bee started. Cheikh leaned over the rail. "Did you memorize the Greek ones like I told you?"

"I studied everything," Caleb said, which wasn't quite true. He'd studied the list Ms. Almeida prescribed every week, but last night he'd gotten stuck on something else. Cheikh had noticed that words from Greek sometimes used "ch" where you'd expect a "k," and words from French used "ch" for the "sh" sound. Caleb had written a page of examples, chorus and chef among them, then fallen asleep on his notes.

The first rounds went fast. A kid in a green hoodie went out on "necessary." Athena spelled "avalanche" without pausing, then sat down and cracked her knuckles, one at a time. Caleb got "civilian," and the judge's voice was flat and quick. "C-I-V-I-L-I-A-N. Civilian." It was a legitimate word, nothing tricky, and he was almost disappointed.

Round five thinned the field to six. Cheikh went out on "bivouac," adding a second "u," and came back to the seats rubbing his face. "I had it," he muttered. "I just said it wrong."

Then the moderator looked at Caleb. "Your word is 'chameleon.'"

"Language of origin?" Caleb asked. That was allowed. He'd seen the older spellers do it at the regional bee last year, and the judges always answered.

"Greek."

The clock ticked on the wall. Caleb thought about his page of notes. Greek, "ch" for the "k" sound, like chorus. So the opening sound here, the "kuh," might be C-H. He wrote it on his palm with one finger, invisible letters. "C-H-A-M-E-L-E-O-N. Chameleon."

"Correct."

Athena looked back at him and raised one eyebrow a tiny amount, which for Athena was a shout.

Round seven, she went out on "bourgeoisie," starting it with a "j" sound that somehow got into her spelling, and shrugged at the ceiling as she walked off the stage. It was down to Caleb, a tall eighth grader named nobody he knew, and the kid in the green hoodie who had somehow survived.

The moderator waited for silence. "Final word. 'Chef.' Language of origin, French."

Caleb's hand was sweating around the card he'd been holding for an hour. He thought again of the page on his desk. French, "sh" sound, spelled "ch." So the whole first sound, the "sh," was C-H. The rest was straightforward. He said it slowly, watching the judge's pen. "C-H-E-F. Chef."

The pen stopped moving. There was a pause that lasted about one breath, and then the judge looked up. "Correct. We have a winner."

Caleb found Cheikh and Athena by the water fountain afterward. Cheikh held out his fist. "Okay, admit it. The Greek thing saved you."

"And the French thing," Caleb said. He tapped the paper cup against the fountain and ice rattled loose. "Same trick, both directions."

"Chorus and chef," Athena said, "both start with C-H, and neither one sounds like it starts with C-H."

"That's the rule," Caleb said, and bumped the cup against hers.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Nervousness triggers the release of adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and pulls blood away from the stomach, causing the "butterflies" feeling.
story:
Hayden's stomach flipped three blocks before the school gym, and his heart was already going like he had sprinted the whole way there. He pressed a hand against his ribs in the passenger seat while his dad drummed the steering wheel at a red light.

"You okay over there?" his dad asked.

"Stomach's weird. Heart's fast too." Hayden frowned. He hadn't even walked in yet. Nothing had happened. Nobody had said anything to him. So why was his body acting like something was already going wrong?

His phone buzzed. Simeon: at the dance, Elody's here, where r u??

Hayden typed back: 5 min. feel sick.

Simeon: everyone feels sick lol. Elody said her heart was pounding when she got here and she wasn't even moving.

Hayden stared at the message. Pounding heart, churning stomach, standing still. That was the same thing, in someone else. It couldn't be an actual illness, then. Illnesses didn't sync up like that across two people at the same dance. It had to be something the situation itself was doing to them, some switch that flipped before anything even happened. He remembered a documentary clip where someone had called it "butterflies," because nerves set off adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and pulls blood away from the stomach. That was the flipping feeling. Not danger. Just blood going somewhere else.

"Can you pull over for a second?" Hayden asked.

His dad blinked but swung the car to the curb. Hayden jumped out, jogged in place for ten seconds, then stopped and breathed slowly, in through his nose, out through his mouth, four counts each. His heart still hammered, but when he thought about the dance on purpose, gym, lights, Elody by the punch table, the flip in his stomach came smaller. His body was reacting to the idea of the place, not the place. He could work with that.

Back in the car, he grinned. "It's like my body tries to convert being nervous into being ready to run. I'm just going to keep breathing and walk in slow."

"That's more insight than I had at your age," his dad said, pulling out. "I threw up in a bush before mine."

At the gym doors, Simeon spotted him and waved him over, wearing the predatory grin he saved for when a teacher was about to hand back a test. "Elody saved you a spot near the speakers," he said. "Fair warning, the chaperone, Ms. Van Dijk, already told me twice to stop looking like that."

Hayden laughed, felt the flip come one more time, let it pass through, and pushed the door open.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Psychologist Lee Ross named the fundamental attribution error in 1977: the tendency to blame others' actions on their personality while underestimating their situation.
story:
Mr. Ramos set a sheet of paper on each desk before the bell finished ringing. "Today's discussion topic," he said, writing on the board, "is what happened in the cafeteria yesterday. You all saw some of it. Sage, start us off."

Sage stood up halfway. "Erin shoved past Tomas at the milk station and knocked his tray off the edge. On purpose, I think. She didn't even say sorry, just walked off with her friends."

Brayden looked across the room at Erin, who was staring at her notebook so hard it seemed like she was trying to burn a hole through it. That didn't match. Yesterday, Brayden had been near the doors when Erin came in, and she had been reading something on her phone with her hand pressed flat over her mouth. He hadn't thought about it at the time.

"I don't think she did it on purpose," Brayden said. "I saw her right before. She looked like she'd just gotten some kind of bad news."

"That's an interesting claim," Mr. Ramos said. "Sage, you saw a shove. Brayden, you saw a distracted kid. Same event." He tapped the board. "Anyone want to test that?"

Brayden raised his hand. "There's this thing my sister told me about. A psychologist named Lee Ross called it the fundamental attribution error. Nineteen seventy-seven. It's how we blame people's actions on their personality and forget their situation." A few kids wrote it down. Sage sat with her arms crossed.

"That's not proof," Sage said. "You're just guessing about her."

"Then let me ask her." Brayden turned in his seat. "Erin, what happened on your phone yesterday?"

Erin looked up. Her voice came out low. "My dad texted me that our dog died. She was old. I was holding my tray and I couldn't see where I was going." She went back to staring at the notebook.

The room went quiet. Someone near the window whispered something about a dead dog being rough, and Brayden thought of the time his own hamster had died, how he had fed that rodant every morning for two years, and how he had walked into a door at school that same afternoon. Sage uncrossed her arms.

"I guess I only saw the shove," Sage said. "I filled in the rest." She paused. "Erin, I'm sorry I said it like that. Not just about the tray."

Mr. Ramos asked the class to write down one time they had judged someone on personality and later learned about their situation. "Try to be impartial with yourselves," he said. "That's the hard part."

Brayden started writing, then stopped. At the end of class, Mr. Ramos would probably call on him again, and if Brayden claimed his sheet was finished before it was, that would be the fundamental attribution error in reverse. He bent back over the paper and kept going.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: In farsightedness, light focuses behind the retina, so near objects look blurry, and it is corrected with convex lenses.
story:
On Saturday morning Emilia sat at the kitchen table with the optometrist's note in front of her, and the note said her new glasses would be ready at five o'clock, exactly one hour before Kaydence's birthday party. That gave her barely any time to learn to live in them before anyone at school saw her on Monday, which felt unfair. The problem wasn't the glasses themselves. The problem was Billie, who had gotten glasses in September and spent a whole week answering questions about them, and Emilia did not want to spend a week answering questions too.

Kaydence came over at noon to help her prepare, which mostly meant sitting on the counter eating crackers while Emilia's mom made a nutritious lunch nobody wanted. "You could just not wear them to the party," Kaydence offered. "No," Emilia said. "I want to actually see the music playlist on my phone instead of holding it at arm's length like my grandmother." That was the strange part, she thought while she sliced an apple. The far wall calendar was crisp, but anything close turned to mush. Somewhere in her eyes, something was landing in the wrong place, the way a projector can throw a picture too far and miss the screen. She couldn't see that happening, but she could reason about it, the way you know a hidden wind by the bending trees.

She tested her idea with her dad's old magnifying glass from the junk drawer. If things focused too far back in her eye, then a lens that bent light inward, toward the middle, might pull the picture forward onto the right spot. She held the curved glass over her brother's comic book and the fuzzy letters snapped into focus. The lens was thicker in the middle than at the edges, bulging outward on both sides, and it worked. She wrote that down, in case the optician thought she was guessing.

At ten past five they picked up the glasses, and in the car Emilia looked in the visor mirror and laughed. Her eyes looked enormous, like a cartoon character's. At the party, Billie leaned across the snack table and frowned at her. "Yours make your eyes bigger," Billie said. "Mine make them smaller. Why?" Emilia considered the two lenses side by side, Billie's thin in the middle, her own thick in the middle, and everything she'd worked out clicked into place. "Because I'm farsighted," she said. "Near stuff is blurry for me, and these bend the light the other way from yours."

Billie studied her for a second, then grinned. "Alliance?" she said, tapping her frames. "Glasses club, no questions allowed, ever." Emilia tapped her own frames back. Kaydence raised her cup of juice between them, and outside the window a string of fairy lights blinked on, sharp and clear all the way down to the last bulb.

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun also gets longer days, giving sunlight more hours to warm the ground.
story:
The trail marker said Heritage Trail, and Mr. Nielsen had promised the class that the loop would integrate a shortcut, which mostly meant climbing over one fallen log instead of two. Jackson didn't care about logs. He cared about one thing: winning the bet with Jerome.

"You said summer's hotter because Earth is closer to the Sun," Jackson had announced at lunch. "I say that's wrong. Bet's a week of my mom's trail mix."

"Not the nutritious kind," Jerome had groaned. "The kind with the chocolate pieces."

They were both wrong, and that was the problem. Kiara had looked it up and refused to tell them anything except one smug sentence: "It's about the tilt." Now, two miles up the trail, Jackson was still chewing on it like a piece of ancient raisin.

"Okay, think," Kiara said, dropping back to walk beside him. "It's July. When does it get dark?"

"After bedtime at summer camp," Jerome said from ahead. "Eight thirty lights out, and it's still bright enough to play catch."

Jackson stopped so fast his boot squeaked. "Wait. That's it. That's the whole thing." He held up his water bottle like a gavel. "In summer the daylight lasts forever. The sun comes up before my alarm and doesn't quit until late. All those extra hours, the ground is just soaking up sunlight and getting warmer and warmer." He pointed at the sun-baked patch of rock beside the trail and then at the cool shaded dirt under the pines. "Feel those. The rock's been in the light all day. The shade hasn't. Same sun, different hours."

"So more hours means hotter," Jerome said slowly.

"And here's the kicker. It works like a see-saw, because the tilt points one half of Earth at the Sun and the other half away. The half tilted toward the Sun gets the longer days, all that time to warm up. The half tilted away gets short days, barely any hours of sunlight, so it stays cold." Jackson grinned. "When it's summer here, it's winter in Australia. Their daylight shrinks while ours grows."

Mr. Nielsen, who had been pretending to study a bird, turned around. "That's a switch, Jackson. Usually you have to be dragged out of the shade."

"Ha. Ha," Jackson said, but he was still grinning. He stuck out his hand to Jerome. "Trail mix. Chocolate kind. Pay up."

Jerome folded his arms. "Not so fast. You said it's about the tilt, fine, but you never said WHY the tilt makes longer days. I want a rematch."

"A rematch on what?"

Jerome smiled the smile of a boy with a plan. "Two weeks. You figure out how a tilt stretches daylight, I figure out anything I want, and whoever's answer is better takes the whole pot." He pulled out a crumpled bag of peanuts, the only nutritious thing in his pack, and shook it like a maraca.

Kiara leaned against the fallen log. "I'll judge. Judges get paid in trail mix."

Jackson looked down the trail, where the afternoon sun was already sliding low, and stuck out his hand. "Deal."

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: In parts of North America, blacklegged ticks, also called deer ticks, can spread Lyme disease, so campers there check their skin and hair for ticks after hiking through woods or tall grass.
story:
Sydney had budgeted exactly three days for missing home, and she refused to run over, which was why she was sitting by the campfire on night one forcing herself to have fun. Calum was toasting a marshmallow he had already set on fire twice. Chanel was telling everyone about a raccoon that had, according to her, opened a cooler with its thumbs. The flames popped, the lake made its soft nighttime noises, and Sydney was almost, almost not thinking about her own bed.

Then Mr. Tesfaye, the camp director, strolled over with his clipboard and said the thing that ruined everything: "Tick checks in the cabins in ten minutes, folks."

Chanel groaned so loudly that a boy across the fire looked up from his fourth marshmallow. "Every night? I brushed my hair this morning. I'm not a nature documentary."

"It's not optional," Mr. Tesfaye said, and moved on toward the next fire pit.

On the walk back, Chanel kept arguing her case to nobody. "I stayed on the trail. Ticks happen to other people. It's basically a fact." Sydney, who had been quietly working through her own assumption, stopped on the cabin steps. She had assumed Chanel skipped trails too, but she'd watched her all day, and Chanel had taken every shortcut through the tall grass behind the dining hall, twice, once to chase a frog. The shortcut was invisible now, but the pattern wasn't.

"Chanel," Sydney said, "you walked through that grass by the dining hall. I saw you."

"That's not grass, that's a lawn."

"It's grass that goes up to your knees."

Inside, the nightly routine was already happening: girls lining up in front of the bathroom mirror while their buddies searched behind ears, along hairlines, behind knees. A counselor named Dana was doing the checklist callout. "Behind the knees, behind the ears, the waistband, the scalp. Deer ticks are tiny, so look close."

"My mom calls them blacklegged ticks," said the girl in front of Sydney, squinting at her buddy's hair. "They can give you Lyme disease. That's the whole reason we check."

Chanel flopped face down on her bunk in protest, so Sydney, who was her buddy, marched over and started on her scalp. Chanel made a sound like a deflating air mattress. Then Sydney found it, a speck near the left ear, small as a poppy seed, and her stomach did a small flip before her brain caught up: speck, moving. "Sit up. Do not panic. I found something."

Chanel sat up so fast the bunk frame squeaked. "Is it a freckle? Tell me it's a freckle."

"It's a freckle with legs."

They took the speck to Dana in a folded tissue, and Dana confirmed it with one glance and tweezers. Chanel was quiet for a full minute, which Calum would later say was a camp record. "Okay," she finally said. "New rule. I check you, you check me, and we never speak of the frog."

"Deal," said Sydney. "But tomorrow I'm walking in the middle of the group."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: In the United States, a large CDC survey found the median age of a girl's first period is about 12 years old, with a wide normal range around it.
story:
Lea dumped the contents of her backpack onto the bedroom floor for the third time that night. Nicola and Liv sat on the bed watching her, a paused video game glowing on the screen behind them.

"You're going to wear a hole in that bag," Nicola said.

"Then I'll patch it." Lea held up the small pencil case she'd been filling. Pads, a spare pair of socks, two quarters for the nurse's office. She'd been carrying it for four months, ever since her older cousin visited and Lea realized she was the only one of them who hadn't started yet. "I just want to be ready."

Liv leaned over the edge of the bed. "You know that's not how it works, right? It's not like a plane where you can regulate the timing. My sister got hers when she was ten. TEN. She thought she was dying."

"My sister was almost fifteen," Nicola said. "She used to say she was the late one in every way, homework, curfew, all of it."

Lea sat back on her heels. Ten and almost fifteen. That was a huge gap. She'd been assuming there was one correct age, and that she was missing it, the way she'd missed the deadline for the field trip form last month. "So which one is normal?"

Liv pulled her phone out from under her pillow. "We looked this up in health, actually. My mom made a whole thing of it. There was this giant CDC survey in the United States, and the median age for a girl's first period was about twelve. But there's a really wide normal range around it."

"Median," Lea repeated.

"Like the middle. Half before, half after."

Lea turned that over. If the middle was twelve and her sister-facts stretched from ten to almost fifteen, then being twelve and not started yet didn't put her anywhere strange. She was somewhere in the middle of a very wide stripe. The pencil case wasn't a shield against being broken; it was just a sensible thing to have, like keeping an umbrella in a locker.

"You look weird," Nicola said. "Like a drone that finally found its propeller."

"I'm not weird. I'm recalibrated."

Liv snorted. "Recalibrated. Sure."

"You're both gullible," Lea said, and zipped the pencil case shut. She slid it into the front pocket of her backpack, the small one, easy to reach, and left the rest of the mess on the floor for morning. Then she grabbed a controller and pointed it at Nicola. "You're winning too much anyway. Unpause it."

Nicola hit the button, and the three of them fell back onto the pillows as the game music started up again.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The first ten amendments to the United States Constitution are called the Bill of Rights, and they were ratified in 1791.
story:
Sarah raced up the community centre steps two at a time, her binder flapping against her hip. Mr. Kaya had promised that whoever explained a right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms the best at Thursday's workshop would get to read their analysis out loud at the community showcase on Saturday, and Sarah wanted that spot more than she wanted lunch, which was saying something.

She skidded into the craft room and dropped her bag next to Roland, who was building a tower out of constitutional flashcards like they were dominoes. "Careful," he said. "The whole legal system could collapse." Zoelie snorted from behind her laptop without looking up.

Mr. Kaya clapped his hands. "Tonight you each pick one right, put it into your own words, and be ready to defend it. Simple." Sarah flipped through her printout of the Charter. Section after section swam at her, all "fundamental freedoms" and "democratic rights," and nothing jumped out. She wanted the perfect one, the one nobody else would pick.

"Pick section two," Roland said. "It's the one about God, so nobody will fight me for it if you don't." Zoelie spun her laptop around. "Okay, hear me out. My cousin in Michigan says her class memorized their rights thing, the first ten amendments to the United States Constitution. They're called the Bill of Rights. Ratified in 1791. She made me quiz her over video chat."

Sarah leaned over the screen. "Wait, they have ten written out separately?" She counted the Charter's sections on her fingers, then counted again, hunting for the equivalent list, the tidy numbered package. There wasn't one. It was like looking for a bus schedule and finding the routes painted on the road instead. She tested her idea out loud: "So theirs is amendments added on, and ours is built in from the start?"

"Sure sounds like it," Zoelie said. "My cousin would faint if she heard you say that so calmly. She had to chant it in a classroom. Twice."

Sarah laughed, then stopped, because a thought had transported her straight out of her nervousness: her cousin was fighting to be allowed to start a girls' skateboard club at her school, and nobody there seemed able to say exactly which right made the "no" illegal. Sarah flipped to freedom of association and read it three times, slowly, like checking whether a bridge would hold. Then she wrote, "This means you get to band together with other people, and no one can shut your group down just because they don't like it," and underlined it twice.

At the showcase on Saturday, she stood at the front of the gym, mic in hand, and found Zoelie's cousin's face in a video chat propped on the front row table. Sarah grinned.

"Hi, Bill of Rights girl," she said. "Want to hear how we do it up here?"

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: When viewing a slide, you start with the lowest-power objective lens to find and focus on the cells before switching to higher power.
story:
The biology lab smelled faintly of onions and glass cleaner, and the microscopes sat in a row along the black counter like patient metal horses. Madison clipped her slide, the one she had made from a papery sliver of onion skin stained purple, and turned straight to the largest objective lens. She pressed her eye to the eyepiece and saw nothing but a soft violet fog. She turned the focus knob slowly, one way and then the other, and the fog only swirled.

"Find your cells yet?" Beatrice asked from the next stool. Beatrice's slide, apparently, was cooperating, because she was already sketching little brick shapes in her notebook.

"No. There's purple mush and that's it." Madison lifted the slide out and checked it against the light. The onion skin was there, thin as a whisper. The problem wasn't the slide. She looked down at the revolving nosepiece with its three lenses of different sizes, and an idea assembled itself in her mind. The big lens showed a tiny, tiny piece of the world, magnified enormously. If she hadn't found the cells yet, hunting for them through the strongest lens would be like searching a whole meadow through a keyhole. It might be more feasible to start the other way around.

She clicked the smallest, lowest-power lens into place and looked again. At first there was still blur, but a wider blur, and when she turned the knob the purple smudge tightened into a lacy grid, cell after cell fitted together like floor tiles. There they were. She moved the stage slowly until a clear one sat in the center of the view, then switched carefully to the middle lens. The cells bloomed larger, walls thick and definite, and inside each one a small dark dot hovered near the edge. The nucleus, she wrote on her diagram, drawing an arrow. She traced the outer boundary of every wall, and labeled the fine line just inside it as the membrane.

"Wait, you're done already?" Maurice leaned over from across the aisle, squinting into his own eyepiece at what was clearly more fog. "I've been focusing forever."

"Quinn," Madison said, keeping her voice low because Ms. Chen was circling the room, "start with the lowest-power lens, find a cell, focus, then go up. Trust me. I tried it the hard way first."

Maurice clicked the smallest lens down, turned the knob twice, and went very still. "Oh," he whispered. "Hello, cells." He began to draw, tongue between his teeth, and Madison returned to her diagram. At the bottom of the page she added a note about antibiotic resistance for the homework question Ms. Chen had assigned, then paraphrased the textbook's sentence in her own words so she would remember it. Under the microscope, the little dark nuclei floated in their purple rooms like small moons.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: The U.S. Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 requires parental consent before websites collect personal information from children under 13, which is why many sites require users to be 13.
story:
Paisley had promised her brother she would figure it out before the end of lunch, and the clock on the lab wall said she had eleven minutes. He sat beside her at the third computer, hunched over a signup page that had rejected him three times already, and every time it did, he typed faster, as if speed could erode the error message away.

"It keeps asking for my birthday," he muttered. "Even when I put it in right."

Paisley leaned over his shoulder. The little blue box was polite about it, the way websites are polite, asking him to confirm his date of birth before it could create his account. Behind them, Jasmine and Aurelia were racing through a typing drill, their keyboards clattering like rain on a tin roof, and Ms. Somsak moved between the rows with her coffee mug, pausing now and then to frown at somebody's screen.

"Let me try something," Paisley said. She was systematic about it, the way she did everything. First attempt: his real birthday, the honest one, March fourth. Rejected. Second attempt: same birthday, one year older. The page paused, thought, and asked again. Third attempt: two years older, which would make him thirteen instead of eleven. The screen went green, and a welcome message bloomed across it like a window opening.

Her brother whooped before she could stop him, and Ms. Somsak appeared behind them almost instantly, mug in hand, reading the screen over Paisley's head. "You changed his birth year," she said. It wasn't a question.

"Only to test it," Paisley said, and it was true. Because now she understood the pattern, the hidden rule the website had been guarding all along. Somewhere she had heard the shape of it, a law from 1998, the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, which requires parental consent before websites collect personal information from children under 13. That was why so many sites required users to be 13. The site wasn't suspicious of her brother. It was checking whether it was allowed to take his information at all.

"Aurelia told me about that last week," Jasmine called from the next row, not even turning around. "Her cousin tried to sign up for the same app and got the same wall."

"Sign out," Ms. Somsak said quietly to Paisley's brother. "You can have an account when you're old enough for one, or with Mom's consent. Not by borrowing a birthday." He sagged in his chair like a scavenger caught raiding the wrong bin, and clicked the logout button.

Paisley saved the page address in her notebook, though, because there was one thing she still wanted to test. If the rule was really about collecting information from children under 13, then maybe there was a way for their mother to say yes on purpose. She wrote that at the bottom of the page, underlined it twice, and slid the notebook into her backpack before the bell could ring.

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
knowledge_domain: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
fact: Shakespeare wrote much of his verse in iambic pentameter: lines of about ten syllables in five pairs, each an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one.
story:
Lincoln slid the paperback across the table until it bumped Ophelie's elbow, because if he had to look at "O that this too too solid flesh would melt" for one more minute alone, he was going to lose it. It was Tuesday, book club, the back room of the library, and Mr. Menon had assigned everyone a speech from Hamlet to turn into "words a person would actually say."

Ophelie read the line out loud, then frowned. "What does he even want? His flesh to melt? That's dark."

"His dad died and his mom married his uncle like a month later," Walker said from across the table, tapping his pencil. "He wants to disappear. So... 'I wish I could just evaporate'?"

Lincoln wrote that down. It worked, but something still bothered him, the same itch he'd felt last week when he'd given up on Romeo and Juliet and just watched the movie instead. He'd skipped the reading, and Mr. Menon had looked at him over his glasses without saying anything, which was somehow worse than a lecture. He kept thinking about that look.

He read the speech again, this time under his breath, and noticed the words had a bounce. "Wait." He put his finger under the first line. "To be, or not to be, that is the question." He tapped the desk as he said it, and his knuckles found a rhythm on the wood, da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM, like a heartbeat or a drum. He counted the taps. Ten. Five pairs, and in every pair the second tap landed harder, like his finger had somewhere to be.

"Try it," he said, and the whole table started tapping, pencils and knuckles, a room full of hearts beating in parallel. Mr. Menon, shelving books by the window, glanced over but didn't interfere.

"There's a name for that," Ophelie said, scrolling on her phone. "Iambic pentameter."

"Every line's about ten syllables," Lincoln said, mostly to himself, still tapping. "That's why it felt like a song even when I didn't get the words." It was almost like finding the hidden logic of a magic trick; once he saw the pattern, the speech stopped being a wall of old English and became something with a pulse.

Walker tried paraphrasing again, keeping the beat, and it came out smoother. "Should I keep living or not, that's what I'm asking." Ophelie laughed and clapped once, then did it again in her own words, tapping along. Lincoln went back to the flesh-melting speech and tapped his way through it, line by line, and the meaning rose to the surface like something radiating heat off a summer sidewalk.

He thought about last week again, the movie, the easy way out, and decided he didn't regret it exactly, but he wouldn't do it that way a second time. Mr. Menon wandered over, listening to the tapping.

"Da-DUM," Lincoln said. "Five times a line."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A percentage based on very few attempts can be misleading: a player who makes one shot out of one attempt shoots 100 percent.
story:
The stat sheet was taped to the rink door, and Maggie stood in front of it with her stick across her shoulders like a bar she'd just lifted. "Perfect shooting percentage," she said. "One hundred percent. Nobody else on this team can say that."

Aaron peeled off his helmet and looked at the column. She was right, in a way. One goal, one shot. Alexander, who kept the numbers in a spiral notebook, had written it in green ink as if it symbolized something holy. Down the list, Aaron himself sat at four goals out of eleven shots, which Alexander had circled and labeled 36 percent in pencil.

"You took one shot," Aaron said. "All season. One."

"It went in," said Maggie.

The locker room smelled like wet wool and the black fungus that grew on the bench by the showers, the one nobody sat on after October. Aaron sat on the other bench and laced his skates, thinking. If one shot counted as a perfect percentage, then the number didn't tell you who could shoot. It told you how many times you'd tried. He decided to test it.

At the next practice, before anyone else was on the ice, he set up ten pucks at the hash marks. The arena was quiet enough that he could hear the refrigeration unit hum under the floor, a sound like the building was slowly thinking. He shot all ten. Six went in. He wrote it down: six of ten, 60 percent. Then, to be fair, he shot one more puck from a bad angle, the kind of shot he'd normally never take. It banked off the post and in. He wrote that down too.

In the locker room after practice, he showed the notebook to Maggie. "I'm at one hundred percent today," he said. "One shot, one goal."

"You shot a million pucks this morning. I watched you."

"That's the point. Percentage alone doesn't say how many attempts it's based on. One out of one is a hundred percent too." He flipped the page to show her the six-of-ten line, then the single-shot line, side by side. "Same number, different amount of evidence."

Mr. Martínez, who drove the Zamboni and sometimes read over their shoulders on his break, leaned in with his coffee. "So who's the better shooter?" he asked.

"I am," said Aaron. "But by her math, we're tied."

Maggie chewed on her mouthguard for a second. "Fine," she said. "I'll take more shots. But if I go one for ten, I'm blaming your notebook."

She took nine shots in the next game. Alexander stood at the glass with his pencil going the whole third period, and their team's playoff hopes, which everyone had called extinct in November, were suddenly, quietly alive again. After the game Maggie found Aaron by the skate sharpener and held out the notebook without a word. Nine shots, three goals. Thirty-three percent.

"Congratulations," said Aaron. "You dropped sixty-seven points."

"And scored two more goals than you did today," said Maggie, and walked off with the stat sheet under her arm.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: The 1996 book 'Continuing Bonds' argued that keeping a connection to someone who has died, through memories, objects or traditions, can be a healthy part of grieving.
story:
Gabriel stood at the edge of the grave with his grandfather's watch in his pocket, and he had about ten minutes to decide. The funeral would end, the casket would go down, and the shovel of earth the minister kept calling imminent would cover everything forever. His mother wanted him to toss the watch in. "He wore it sixty years," she whispered. "It should go with him."

His friend Emerick had come along, mostly because Emerick came to everything, and now he stood beside Gabriel squinting at the wreaths. "So are you going to throw it in?"

"That's what I have to evaluate," Gabriel said. "Whether keeping it means I'm, like, refusing to let go. Whether that's bad for me." He turned the watch over. The crystal was scratched from some long-ago fall, and the leather strap had gone soft as an old dog's ear.

Behind them, Mr. Kaur, who had lived next door to Grandpa for thirty years, cleared his throat. "You know, when my father died, I kept his prayer cap," he said. "A librarian friend put a book in my hands. Continuing Bonds, it was called. 1996. It argued that keeping a connection to someone who has died, through memories, objects, traditions, can be a healthy part of grieving." He tugged his own sleeve straight. "I read it twice."

Gabriel stared at him. "So it's not weird? Keeping the watch?"

"It's a bond," Mr. Kaur said. "Bonds don't get buried with the body. But it's your watch to decide about." He moved off to speak to Gabriel's mother, and Gabriel heard him telling her quietly that Emerick's ride hadn't shown up, and that he'd drive the boy home himself so Gabriel's family wouldn't have to worry about it.

Gabriel crouched and pressed two fingers to the grass beside the grave. The soil underneath was dark and cold. Somewhere in there, microbes would do their slow work on wood and cloth, and Gabriel tried to picture whether a watch counted as part of Grandpa or just a thing he'd owned. A thing could break down into soil. The smell of Grandpa's workshop, the way he hummed while soldering, the joke about the three engineers in the bar, those did not break down. Those were the bond.

The minister stepped forward. The casket waited on its straps. Gabriel took the watch out, buckled it onto his own wrist, where it hung loose and ticking, and pressed the crown once, the way Grandpa always did before bed.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Details in the background of a photo, such as a street sign, a house number or a school logo, can let a stranger work out where it was taken.
story:
Ivy slid her phone under the table and opened the selfie one more time. She had taken it on the front porch after school, grinning with her new haircut, and she wanted to post it before Jovan's party photos took over everyone's feeds. At the dinner table her father was asking about homework, and her little brother was dropping noodles on the floor in a way that made her despise family dinners.

"Ivy. Phone away," her father said.

"Two minutes." She zoomed in to check her hair, and then she saw it, small and white at the edge of the frame. Their house number, 47, right beside the porch door. Behind it, faintly, the green street sign at the corner. She zoomed further. Riverside Lane. Anyone looking at the photo could read both, and anyone who read both would know exactly where she lived.

She scrolled back through everything she had ever posted. The picture from the school bake sale had the banner with the school logo hanging behind Everleigh's shoulder. The one from the park showed the entrance sign and its address carved into the stone. Even the video of her dog had, for three seconds at the start, the front of the house with the number again. She had been meticulous about her hair, her angle, her captions, and careful about none of this.

"You're quiet," her father said. "That's new."

"Everleigh commented on my park photo. Said she found the exact bench." Ivy put the phone flat on the table, screen up. "Look. This was from March. You can see the address on the sign."

Her father leaned over. Her brother leaned too, chewing.

"So?" her brother said.

"So a stranger could do the same thing Everleigh did. Find the bench, find the park, find us." She flicked to the porch selfie and zoomed until the number filled the corner of the screen. "Forty-seven. Anyone who sees this knows our house."

Her father set down his fork. "Delete it."

"I didn't post it yet. But the others are already out there. Everleigh found the bench from one sign. Somebody else could do the same with our street." She started tapping, deleting the park photo, then the bake sale, then the dog video, her thumb moving fast.

Her brother reached for her phone. "Can I see the dog one before you kill it?"

"Too late." She turned the phone toward him to show the empty gallery, then pulled it back. "I'm going to tell Jovan tomorrow. He posts his front porch all the time."

Her father carried his plate to the sink. "Tell Everleigh too."

Ivy looked at the last picture left in the camera roll, the unposted selfie, and pinched the screen until the house number and the street sign sat just outside the frame. She typed a message to Jovan: check your porch pics. Then she hit send.

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: A meeting chair decides who speaks next and usually calls on someone who has not spoken yet before letting someone speak again.
story:
Aaron tapped the agenda paper against the picnic table until the noise circle quieted down. He had written three items at breakfast: trail cleanup, the bird count, and the campfire skit. Nine campers sat on logs around him, and Mr. Halvorsen leaned against a tree nearby, watching but saying nothing.

"First item, trail cleanup," Aaron began. Viviane's hand shot up, and Katelynn's followed half a second later. He called on Viviane, who talked for two solid minutes about gloves. Then Katelynn added her point about gloves, which was basically equivalent to Viviane's point, just longer. When they finished, four other hands were still raised, including a small kid from Cabin Four who had been stretching his arm up so long it had begun to shake.

Viviane's hand went up again. "One more thing about the gloves," she said.

Aaron hesitated. Calling on her again felt rude, but she was his friend, and nobody had told him the rules for this. He nodded at her, and she talked some more. When she stopped, the Cabin Four kid's hand was still up, but so was Katelynn's, and Katelynn was already saying, "Okay, but the trash bags," before he'd chosen anyone at all. The small kid slowly lowered his hand and stared at his shoes.

Aaron's stomach twisted. He glanced at the agenda, then at the circle, and made a quick diagnosis of the meeting so far: the same two people had spoken four times, and half the circle had spoken zero times. He thought back to the student council meeting he'd sat in on last spring. The president had kept looking around the room before each turn, and he had always picked someone new. Aaron realized the chair was the one who decided who spoke next, not whoever talked loudest or fastest.

"Viviane," he said when she raised her hand a third time, "I'm going to hold that, because some people haven't gotten a turn yet." He turned toward Cabin Four. "You've had your hand up forever. What were you going to say?"

"There's a wasp nest by the bridge," the kid said, voice wobbling. "Nobody should clean there without the spray can."

The circle went silent, then erupted. That was exactly the kind of thing they needed. Aaron wrote "wasp nest, bridge" on the agenda under trail cleanup. After that, he kept his eyes moving around the circle, picking raised hands in a pattern he could defend: a new speaker before a repeat speaker. He did let Viviane talk again later, after three others had gone, and she kept it short. Katelynn nudged the Cabin Four kid and offered him the second pair of her own gloves for bridge duty.

By the time they reached the campfire skit item, everyone in the circle had spoken at least twice, and the kid from Cabin Four was volunteering to play the raccoon. Mr. Halvorsen pushed off from the tree, gave Aaron a small nod, and walked toward the dining hall.

"Same time tomorrow," Aaron said, and folded the agenda into his pocket.

activity: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
knowledge_domain: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
fact: The blues scale is the minor pentatonic scale with one extra note, the flattened fifth, which gives the music its gritty 'blue' sound.
story:
Nora's saxophone had a sound like a goose with a grievance, and everyone in the storage room behind the band hall knew it. She was supposed to improvise a blues solo over the twelve-bar progression for Friday's assembly, and so far her solo had four notes in it, all safe, all dull. Maksim sat on an upturned tuba case eating pretzels while she ran the changes again. "That's a solo the way a fence is a vacation," he said.

She glared at him and played the four notes again, louder. The backing track on the classroom's old laptop ground on, guitar chords cycling past in their patient order, and Nora felt like she was standing outside a locked house trying every key on a ring. Rex leaned in the doorway with a trumpet case balanced on his hip. "You're restricting yourself to the pentatonic," he said. "Five notes. Safe. My cousin calls it the fence too, by the way."

"That helps me zero," Nora said, but it helped her a little, because it gave her a thought. She knew the five-note pattern cold. The solo sounded fine and completely unlike the recordings Mr. Popescu played them, the ones with the gritty, scraped-raw sound that had made her want to do this in the first place. Something was in those recordings that was not in her five notes. A stranger's note. She considered the context of everything she'd heard: the players didn't sound like they were breaking rules. They sounded like they were using one she hadn't found.

So she tested a simple idea. She slid down a half step from the fifth note of her pattern and landed on the note just below it, flat where it should have been sharp-edged and clean. Then she played it again, bent and growling, right over the fourth bar. Maksim stopped chewing. "What was that," he said, which was not a question.

"It's the flattened fifth," Nora said. "You add it to the five notes, and it stops sounding like an exercise and starts sounding like the blues." She ran the solo again, and this time the strange note snarled through the middle of every phrase, and even the goose-grief squeak in her low register sounded intentional, almost stylish. Rex raised his trumpet case in a slow salute.

On Friday, in front of an audience that included the affluent families who donated the new risers, Nora stood up for her eight bars. She played her fence of five notes, then let the flat one loose, and heard a woman in the second row say "oh" out loud. Maksim, in the clarinet section, held up one pretzel in silent tribute.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Psychologist John Suler described the 'online disinhibition effect' in 2004: people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face.
story:
The comment appeared at 9:47 on Tuesday night, in the group chat for the science fair: "Honestly Anabel your poster looks like a kindergartner made it. Maybe let someone with taste handle the design." It was signed, in a way, by the name at the top of the bubble: Walid. Vincent stared at his phone. Walid was the kid who said "excuse me" to desks he bumped into, who had helped Anabel carry her poster board up two flights of stairs that very afternoon.

Anabel didn't reply in the chat. On Wednesday she sat alone at lunch, poking at her pasta, and when Vincent asked if she was okay she said, "Fine," which was obviously not true. He kept replaying the message. The Walid on the stairs and the Walid in the chat couldn't be the same person, could they? But it wasn't a hack; the account had been his for years, complete with his dog in the profile picture.

Vincent decided to test a simple idea: that people act differently in writing than they do in person, and that the difference might be a known thing, something with a name. During study hall he searched "why are people mean online but nice in person." Most of what came up was junk, but one result looked plausible, a paper by a psychologist named John Suler. It described what he called the online disinhibition effect, the way people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face. Vincent wrote down the citation so he could show Anabel the source, then screenshotted the paragraph and incorporated it into his notes with the screenshot of Walid's comment, side by side like evidence at a trial.

The next morning he found Walid at his locker. "Did you mean what you wrote about Anabel's poster?" Vincent asked. Walid's face went pale, then red. "I was frustrated about the layout. I typed it without thinking. I would never say that to her, though. Not to her face." That was the part that interested Vincent, and the part that made it worse. It wasn't an impostor. It was Walid, minus whatever stops him in the hallway.

They walked to the computer lab together and found Ms. Lindqvist monitoring the morning crowd. Walid said he would apologize, and he typed it into the chat right there, with his hands shaking a little: "Anabel, that comment was wrong. Your poster is great and I'm sorry." The bubble turned blue and delivered. Then Anabel replied, a single thumbs-up, no words, and closed her phone. At the science fair on Friday she stood beside her poster, which was beautiful, and she thanked the judges politely, and when Walid brought her a cup of punch she took it and said, "Thanks," but she stood a little apart from him the whole evening, and she didn't rejoin the group chat until the following week.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Deleting a post removes it from your page, but anyone who already took a screenshot or saved a copy still has it.
story:
At dinner, Emmett pushed his noodles around the plate while his phone sat face-down beside his glass, buzzing like a trapped wasp. He had posted a video of himself doing a terrible magic trick that afternoon, realized within ten minutes how bad it looked, and deleted it. Now the buzzing wouldn't stop. His dad asked twice whether the chicken needed more salt before Emmett finally flipped the phone over.

The screen showed the group chat with Tristan, Lindsey, and half the soccer team. Lindsey had sent a clip. Emmett tapped it, and there he was again, mid-trick, dropping the cards, his face frozen in the exact moment before the trick failed. He checked his own page first, scrolling fast. The post was gone, deleted, exactly as he'd left it. Yet there it was in the chat, playing on a loop. He typed, "I deleted that," and Tristan answered in seconds: "Lindsey saved it before you did. Anyone who grabs a copy keeps it." Emmett read the line three times. Deleting had felt like slamming a door, but the room had already been photographed.

He set the phone down and tried an experiment in his head. If deleting only cleaned up his page, then anything he posted, photos, his location at the pizza place, everything, could already be sitting in somebody's camera roll, somebody he didn't even know. He picked up the phone and asked Lindsey directly, "Who else has this?" A typing bubble appeared, then vanished, then appeared again. "Just the team," she wrote, which was not exactly an answer. His mom, watching his neutral expression go pale, slid the water pitcher toward him without a word.

"I need to ask people to delete their copies," Emmett said aloud, half to his plate. His dad asked what was going on, and Emmett showed him the chat. "Deleting a post removes it from your page, but anyone who already took a screenshot or saved a copy still has it," his dad said, reading Tristan's message back slowly. Emmett nodded. That was the rule, and he hadn't known it existed until it stepped on him.

He messaged everyone in the chat, one at a time, asking politely. Most complied. Tristan sent back a thumbs-up and then, a minute later, "Done." Emmett felt his shoulders drop an inch. Lindsey sent a heart and promised the copies were gone.

At breakfast the next morning, his phone buzzed once. It was Lindsey: "Ask your mom to check the family photo stream." Emmett stared at the message, then opened the app, and there, between his grandmother's birthday cake and the lake vacation, was his own blurry face, mid-trick, cards raining onto the carpet, saved automatically by the cloud. He sighed, grabbed a slice of toast, and went to find his mom. "So," he said, holding up the phone, "how do I delete something I never posted?"

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: A red herring is a false clue placed on purpose to lead readers toward the wrong conclusion, so not every hint in a story is real foreshadowing.
story:
Rebecca spread the photocopied story across her grandmother's kitchen table, weighting the corners with a jar of pickles and a tin of shortbread. "Book club starts in five minutes," she announced. "Grandma said we could use the kitchen as long as we don't spill anything near her recipes."

Damian arrived first, clutching his copy like a warrant for arrest. "The ending is so obvious," he declared before he'd even sat down. "Page two, Mrs. Vale keeps staring at the locked cabinet. That's foreshadowing. She's the thief. Case closed." Quentin slouched in behind him, eating the last of the shortbread, and shrugged in a way that suggested he had opinions but was saving them.

Rebecca had read the story three times the night before, curled in her grandmother's reading chair while the clock downstairs ticked like a slow heartbeat. Damian's evidence bothered her. The cabinet appeared on page two, sure, and again on page five, and yet the whole story seemed to revolve around the neighbor's greenhouse, where half the conversations happened. Why would the writer keep dragging them back to the greenhouse if the cabinet mattered so much?

"Okay," she said, flipping pages. "Let's test it. If the cabinet is a real clue, then the thief has to have a way in, a reason, and a moment alone with it." She traced the timeline with her pencil. Mrs. Vale never had a moment alone. She was always in the greenhouse, reviving drooping orchids, talking about the flower commerce at the village market, handing out spontaneous advice to strangers. Meanwhile the cousin, quiet little footnote of a character, was mentioned twice bringing in the mail.

Quentin sat up. "The mail. The mail!" He grabbed Damian's copy and stabbed the paragraph. "The key arrives in the mail. Page four."

"The cabinet, though," Damian insisted, but his voice had developed a wobble.

"Think about it," Rebecca said. "The writer put the cabinet right up front, big and shiny and suspicious, so we'd all stare at it and miss the cousin. That's a red herring." Damian opened his mouth, and she held up a hand. "A false clue placed on purpose to lead readers toward the wrong conclusion. Not every hint in a story is real foreshadowing. Sometimes the writer is tricking you."

There was a silence, into which the back door opened and Mr. Lee from next door leaned in, holding a trowel. "Grandmother said something about a book club? I've read that one." He settled into a chair without waiting for an answer. "Fell for the cabinet myself, first time through. Threw the book across the room at the end."

"You too?" Damian groaned, and dropped his forehead onto the table beside the pickle jar. Quentin patted his shoulder with mock solemnity and offered him the empty shortbread tin, as if it were a prize for effort.

Rebecca read the final paragraph aloud, and there it was, the cousin slipping the key into his pocket, hidden in a sentence about orchids. "So what does the greenhouse mean?" she asked, pencil ready. "Because that orchid that keeps nearly dying? I think it's the whole point."

Damian lifted his head. "Explain that again," he said, "slowly, and this time I'm taking notes."

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: In Mexican tradition, a quinceañera, the celebration of a girl's fifteenth birthday, usually begins with a Mass of thanksgiving.
story:
The cemetery behind St. Augustine's was the quietest place James knew, so that was where he practiced. He sat on the flat stone near his grandfather's plot with the paper folded in his pocket, saying the words out loud to nobody. His friend Sonia had asked him for help, because in two weeks she would turn fifteen, and her quinceañera, the big Mexican celebration, would begin with a Mass of thanksgiving at the church. Sonia had to do a reading at that Mass, and she could not get through it without stopping.

"You're the one who memorized the whole Gettysburg Address in fifth grade," she had said, handing him the paper. "Figure out why my brain won't hold this."

James had a theory about memorizing, and he wanted to test it. He believed you could not really quantify memory by counting repetitions, the way you'd count jumping jacks. Instead, he thought the brain remembered rhythm and breaks, the places where a sentence turned. So in the cemetery he tried reading the passage in strange chunks, stopping in the middle of phrases instead of at the periods, and then trying the normal way. The strange way was harder, which surprised him. His theory said the pauses were the anchors, and the experiment seemed to prove it.

When Sonia came to the cemetery after school the next day, her entrance was so abrupt that a crow bolted off the fence. "Sorry," she said, breathless. "My mom sent me with the list of everything that still costs money. The hall, the cake, the photographer. She keeps calling the cake delivery a tariff, like the cake is imported from another country." James laughed, then got serious. "Try the reading, but pause wherever I tap." He tapped at odd places, and she tripped over the words, exactly as he predicted. Then he tapped only at the sentence breaks, and the passage rolled out of her like water finding a downhill path.

"That was it," Sonia said, staring at him. "The pauses. When I pause in the wrong spot, I lose the thread and can't find it again."

They met in the cemetery every evening that week, trading lines back and forth while the shadows stretched across the graves. Sonia made mistakes, and James made worse ones, once mangling a line so badly she laughed until she cried. Ms. Quinn, the church's music teacher, passed by on Thursday and heard Sonia run the whole reading clean. "Again," she said simply, and Sonia did it again, perfect.

On the morning of the Mass, James sat in the third pew, his hands folded tight. Sonia walked to the lectern in her pale dress, took a breath, and paused where the pauses belonged. Her voice carried all the way to the back of the church, and James mouthed every word along with her, silently, from his seat.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: When each person pays for their own share of a bill, it is often called 'going Dutch'.
story:
Sophoria had spent all Saturday morning turning the kitchen counter into a café. She folded a paper menu, arranged her grandmother's old teacups, and taped a sign to the toaster that said SOPEN'S CAFE, which was meant to say SOPHIA'S CAFE but she had run out of room for the A. Deklan was coming over at two o'clock, and technically it was a date, because he had asked, "Do you want to go on a date?" and she had said, "Okay," and then both of them had turned bright red about it.

The problem was money. She had eleven dollars and forty cents in the flowered tin on her desk, and she had worked out a whole algorithm for the afternoon: three dollars for fancy hot chocolate ingredients, two dollars back into the tin for emergencies, and the rest hidden under her pillow where she wouldn't be tempted. But the algorithm had never answered the big question. If Deklan showed up with five dollars of his own, who paid for what? On a date, did one person pay for everything? Would he expect her to? What if he paid and she felt like she owed him a cookie forever?

She called Charly, who knew everything about everything, or at least claimed to.

"Whoever invited the other person pays," Charly said immediately. Then Charly paused, which was unusual. "Or no. My cousin says both people pay. She read it in a magazine."

"That makes no sense. Then it's not even a date, it's just two people buying their own stuff."

"I'm telling you what the magazine said," Charly said. "Ask Ms. He. She's been on like a million dates. Probably. She has a velvet hat."

Ms. He was the neighbour on the corner, an eccentric retired music teacher who wore that velvet hat in all weather and once marched a tuba down the street for no reason anyone ever learned. Sophia envied her a little, the way she did things without seeming to worry about them first. Ms. He was in her garden pulling up something green when Sophia trotted over, and she listened to the whole money problem while holding a carrot like a microphone.

"Well," Ms. He said, "when each person pays for their own share, it's called going Dutch."

Sophia stared at her. "Going Dutch. Like the country."

"That's what they call it," Ms. He said, and went back to her carrots as if she had not just solved the entire afternoon.

At two o'clock Deklan arrived with his hair combed, which was the funniest thing Sophia had seen all week, and Charly showed up ninety seconds later wearing an apron and announcing that she was the waiter and would accept tips in gum. Charly took the fake orders, brought the hot chocolate, and then presented a bill on a folded piece of paper that said 4 DOLLERS, and the awkward moment landed exactly where Sophia had feared. Deklan reached for his pocket. Sophia reached for the tin. Their hands hovered.

"Going Dutch," Sophia said, and slid one dollar across the counter toward Charly, who made a big show of pinching the bill and tucking it into the apron.

"Excellent choice," Charly said, and then dropped the entire tray of cookies on the floor.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: Historians sort reasons for migration into push factors, which drive people away from home, and pull factors, which attract them to a new place.
story:
Aurora found the diary in the wooden trunk at her grandmother's house, wedged between a quilt and a tin of buttons. The cover read "Journal of H. Tatum, 1849." She texted Clemence and Chelsey immediately, because Mr. Horváth had assigned exactly this: use a primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s, and presentations were on Thursday.

"You found an actual diary?" Clemence shouted when they arrived the next morning, bike helmets still on. Chelsey was already pulling on gloves, because Aurora had said the pages were fragile. They spread the diary on the kitchen table while Aurora's grandmother made cocoa, and the three of them leaned over the tiny, slanted handwriting.

The first entry changed everything. "Our farm in Missouri failed two seasons running," H. Tatum had written. "Grain sells for nothing here, and the fever took our neighbor's eldest boy." Chelsey tapped the page. "Those are reasons to leave home." A few entries later, Tatum wrote about letters from a cousin in Oregon describing rich soil and free land, and Clemence threw up her hands. "Those are reasons to go there. It's like the family got pushed out of Missouri and pulled west."

"That's the thing," Aurora said, grabbing her notebook. "Mr. Horváth called them push factors and pull factors. Historians sort reasons for migration that way." She drew two columns and headed one PUSH and one PULL. "Failed crops, no money, sickness, those go on the push side. Free land and good soil, that's pull." She paused. "But some entries don't fit either column. Tatum writes that his wife's brother already went west. Which side is that?"

Chelsey argued it was a pull, because family attracted them. Clemence said it was subjective, that the same reason could feel like a pull to Tatum but nothing at all to his wife, and maybe even a push if staying meant losing her brother forever. Aurora wrote it in a third column labeled QUESTION MARK. "Good," she said. "Mr. Horváth likes when we show the messiness of real evidence. A diary is one person's view, not the whole story."

They worked through eleven entries, and something else surfaced. The Tatums listed their reasons in order, money first, land second, family last. "It's a hierarchy," Clemence said, jabbing the page. "They even ranked their own reasons." Aurora copied the ranked list onto a poster board, then had each of them read one entry aloud so nothing was missed.

When Aurora's grandmother came back with cocoa, she admitted she had never disclosed the trunk's whole history; the diary had come from a great-great-aunt, and there might be letters in the attic, too. Aurora was already halfway up the stairs, flashlight in hand, Chelsey and Clemence pounding behind her. "If we find letters," she called over her shoulder, "we can check whether the Tatums' diary matches what they told the family back home."

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: A damp cloth or damp paper towel under a cutting board stops the board from sliding across the counter while you chop.
story:
Emile held the knife the way Ms. Jung had shown them, fingers curled under like a claw, knuckles forward. The onion sat on the cutting board, pale and smug, waiting to make him cry. Across the counter, Amal was already dicing hers into neat little squares, and Mathew had dismantled his onion into rings without chopping anything at all.

"One more station needs a sauce base," Ms. Jung called out, "so pace yourselves."

Emile pressed down with the knife and the whole board skidded sideways, sliding toward the edge of the counter. He caught it with his hip before the onion rolled off. He tried again, and again the board slid. Amal glanced over. "Yours is going for a walk," she said.

"It does that every time I push down." Emile frowned at the board. It was a durable plastic one, hardly worn, and the counter was clean and dry. That was the thing, he thought. At home his mother's old wooden board never moved, but that counter had a textured surface. This one was smooth as glass. When he pressed, something invisible was letting the board glide, like a tiny sled. He tested it with his palm, pushing gently. Yep, it slid with almost no effort.

He looked around. Mathew was wiping down his station with a damp cloth. Emile grabbed a paper towel, ran it under the tap, wrung it out, and laid it flat under his cutting board. Then he set the onion back on top and pressed down with the knife. The board stayed planted. He chopped once, twice, and the rounds fell away without a single skid.

"Hey, that's clever," Mathew said, leaning over. "A wet towel under the board?"

"Stops it sliding," Emile said, already working the claw grip through the next slice. His eyes stung, but a smaller percentage of the onion was still whole now, which meant fewer fumes rising at once, or so it seemed. Amal came around with her pot, watching him work.

"Half-centimeter pieces," she said. "Those are actually good."

"Sauce crew, assembly in five," Ms. Jung announced.

Emile swept his onion into the pan Amal held out, and the pieces hit the oil with a hiss. Mathew fetched the canned tomatoes, and soon the whole station smelled like something worth eating. Emile chopped a second onion for the pot without once chasing the board across the counter.

"Same towel trick next week?" Mathew asked, holding up the dripping paper towel.

"Every week," Emile said, and dropped it in the trash.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Two people can agree on every fact about an event and still interpret it differently because they value different things, such as fairness versus loyalty.
story:
Ms. Hernández wrote one question on the board before the bell had even finished ringing: "Did Marcus do the right thing?" Marcus was a fictional boy from a short story they had all read, a teammate who lied to a coach to cover for his friend Dev, whose grades had slipped. The robotics club had voted on it yesterday and nearly split in two, and Ms. Hernández had clearly decided to make her class do the same thing.

"Vote at the end of the period," she said. "You have forty minutes to figure out why you disagree, not just that you disagree. If you can't tell me that, the whole class loses the debate on Friday." That was the deal, and everyone groaned, because the Friday debate was the fun one.

Cassia went first, arms crossed. "He protected his friend. Dev would have been benched, and Marcus knew it." Titus rolled his eyes so far Nora thought they might not come back. "He lied to the coach. That's it. You don't lie to the coach."

Nora, who had been put in charge of writing down the club's arguments because she was the only one with legible handwriting, started doing what she usually did: listing the facts. Marcus lied. He lied to protect Dev. Dev was benched anyway. The team found out. She read the list out loud, and then something odd happened. Nobody argued with a single item.

"Wait," Nora said. "You both agree on all of this?"

"Obviously," said Titus.

"Obviously," said Cassia, at the same moment, which was the first thing they had agreed on all week.

Nora tried an experiment. She flipped to a new page and wrote Marcus lied to protect his friend at the top, then asked each of them the same question: "What's the bad part?" Titus circled the word lied. Cassia circled the words to protect his friend, then drew a little heart around them, which Nora felt undermined her seriousness, but she let it go.

"You're not arguing about what happened," Nora said slowly, testing the idea out loud before she trusted it. "You're arguing about what matters. Titus cares about the rule. Cassia cares about the friend."

"It's called fairness," Titus said.

"It's called loyalty," said Cassia.

They glared at each other, both correct. Nora looked at the clock. Twelve minutes left. She raised her hand, and when Ms. Hernández called on her, Nora read both circles aloud and proposed an amendment to their plan: instead of arguing who was right, the class would argue fairness versus loyalty itself, incorporating both positions as its own side. Ms. Hernández raised one eyebrow, which from her was applause.

"Vote," she said.

It passed, eleven to nine. Titus and Cassia were the last two hands up, and they raised them at exactly the same time.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: On a distance-time graph, a straight sloping line means the object is moving at a constant speed.
story:
Livia had forty minutes before the judges reached her table, and her graph was still wrong. She unrolled the paper and pinned it flat: nine points she had marked last night, scattered like spilled beads instead of sitting in any kind of line. Her project was a rubber ball rolled down the school hallway, timed with a stopwatch at one metre, two metres, three metres and so on. The table beside it read "How Fast Does It Roll?" and so far the honest answer was that she had no idea.

"Your dots are all over the place," said Maximilian, leaning over from the next table, where his robust volcano waited for its final coat of paint. He had supervise duty for the hallway timing yesterday because he owed her for the time she'd covered his paper route, and he had stood there clicking the stopwatch while muttering about it, which had bred in her a small, stubborn resentment she hadn't bothered to argue away.

"The clicks were late," Livia said. "You clicked late."

"Late every single time? Exactly the same amount?" He set down his paintbrush. "Roll it here. I'll time it again, right now, and you watch."

She cleared a path between their tables. The gym floor was smooth wax, better than the hallway's bumpy tile. Livia crouched, called "go," and pushed the ball with the same steady shove she'd used before. Maximilian clicked at each metre mark she'd taped down, and Eli, who had wandered over from the refreshments table, wrote the numbers on a napkin. They ran it three times. The numbers came out close to the first set, close enough that her stomach dropped. It wasn't the timing.

She plotted the new points quickly, one after another, before she could lose her nerve. This time she drew it on fresh paper, distance along the bottom, time going up. When she connected the dots, they climbed in a clean, even path from the lower left to the upper right. No wobble. She checked the old graph again and found the mistake: last night she had plotted two of her metres in the wrong columns, transposed like a bad text message.

"Look at this," she said to Eli, holding up the new sheet. "A straight sloping line. That means the ball is moving at a constant speed." Eli frowned at it, then at the ball, then back at the paper, as if the line and the rubber sphere had to be the same object.
